title: How to "DODGE" Complex Software Analytics

edges.target: FFtrees for SE analytics (Chen et al., FSE'18)
edges.ref: [15] D. Chen et al., "Applications of psychological science for actionable analytics," Foundations of Software Engineering, 2018.
edges.evidence: Fig. 8: RQ2 results. Defect prediction results for DODGE(.2), N = 30 vs (FFtrees, SMOTUNED, DE+RF, RANDOM).

edges.target: FFtrees for SE analytics (Chen et al., FSE'18)
edges.ref: [15] D. Chen et al., "Applications of psychological science for actionable analytics," Foundations of Software Engineering, 2018.
edges.evidence: this paper includes the prior results with that of Chen et al. results [15] ... our experimental rig repeats numerous prior studies (this time adding in DODGE(E)).

edges.target: d2h 'distance to heaven' metric (Chen et al.)
edges.ref: [15] D. Chen et al., "Applications of psychological science for actionable analytics," Foundations of Software Engineering, 2018.
edges.evidence: D2h, or "distance to heaven", shows how close scores fall to "heaven" (where recall=1 and false alarms (FPR)=0) [15].

edges.target: FFTrees toolbox / depth-4 advice (Phillips et al.)
edges.ref: [51] N. D. Phillips, H. Neth, J. K. Woike, and W. Gaissmaier, "Fftrees: A toolbox to create, visualize, and evaluate fast-and-frugal decision trees," JDM, 2017.
edges.evidence: Following the advice of [15], [51], we generate trees of depth of d = 4.

edges.target: Fast-and-frugal trees (Martignon et al.)
edges.ref: [33] L. Martignon, K. V. Katsikopoulos, and J. K. Woike, "Categorization with limited resources: A family of simple heuristics," J. Math. Psych., 2008.
edges.evidence: Fast and Frugal Trees (FFtrees) were developed by psychological scientists [33] trying to generate succinct, easily comprehensible models.

edges.target: SMOTUNED (Agrawal & Menzies, ICSE'18)
edges.ref: [3] A. Agrawal and T. Menzies, "Is better data better than better data miners?: on the benefits of tuning smote for defect prediction," ICSE, 2018.
edges.evidence: SMOTUNED is Agrawal et al. ICSE'18 [3]'s hyperparamater optimizer that tunes SMOTE ... Figure 8 compares hyperparameter optimizers with DODGE(.2)

edges.target: Agrawal & Menzies ICSE'18: tuning options, CK metric definitions, statistical protocol
edges.ref: [3] A. Agrawal and T. Menzies, "Is better data better than better data miners?: on the benefits of tuning smote for defect prediction," ICSE, 2018.
edges.evidence: Options in learners from recent SE papers on hyperparameter optimization [2], [3], [22], [24] ... For definitions on code metrics, please refer table 1 of [3].

edges.target: Minkowski p>2 finding (Agrawal et al.)
edges.ref: [3] A. Agrawal and T. Menzies, "Is better data better than better data miners?: on the benefits of tuning smote for defect prediction," ICSE, 2018.
edges.evidence: a standard default is p = 2. Yet Agrawal et al. [3] found that p > 2 worked much better for their processing.

edges.target: DE+RF differential-evolution tuned random forest (Fu et al.)
edges.ref: [23] W. Fu, V. Nair, and T. Menzies, "Why is differential evolution better than grid search for tuning defect predictors?" CoRR abs/1609.02613, 2016.
edges.evidence: DE+RF is a hyperparameter optimizer proposed by Fu et al. [23] that uses differential evolution to tune the control parameters of random forests.

edges.target: Tuning for software analytics with DE (Fu et al., IST'16)
edges.ref: [22] W. Fu, T. Menzies, and X. Shen, "Tuning for software analytics: Is it really necessary?" Information and Software Technology, 2016.
edges.evidence: DODGE(E) also did better than the IST'16 journal article that demonstrated the value of tuning for learners [22] by about 30% and 10%

edges.target: Tuning ranges / DE justification (Fu et al., IST'16)
edges.ref: [22] W. Fu, T. Menzies, and X. Shen, "Tuning for software analytics: Is it really necessary?" Information and Software Technology, 2016.
edges.evidence: SMOTUNED and DE+RF used DE since (a) DE can handle numeric and discrete options; and (b) it has proven useful in prior SE studies [22].

edges.target: 32 classifiers in 4 rank groups (Ghotra et al., ICSE'15)
edges.ref: [24] B. Ghotra, S. McIntosh, and A. E. Hassan, "Revisiting the impact of classification techniques on the performance of defect prediction models," ICSE, 2015.
edges.evidence: DODGE(E) out-performed an ICSE'15 article exploring different learners for defect prediction [24] by around 50% and 40% for d2h and Popt(20)

edges.target: Learner selection from Ghotra et al. rank groups
edges.ref: [24] B. Ghotra, S. McIntosh, and A. E. Hassan, "Revisiting the impact of classification techniques on the performance of defect prediction models," ICSE, 2015.
edges.evidence: Ghotra et al. [24] was used to guide learner selection ... We picked at random from each of their ranks to select SL, NB, EM, SMO

edges.target: LDADE tuned topic modeling (Agrawal, Fu, Menzies, IST'18)
edges.ref: [2] A. Agrawal, W. Fu, and T. Menzies, "What is wrong with topic modeling? and how to fix it using search-based software engineering," IST, vol. 98, 2018.
edges.evidence: LDADE FFT and LDADE SVM both used differential evolution [55] ... DODGE(E) performs better than the IST'18 journal article ... [2] by about 20%

edges.target: PITS vectorization / LDA protocol and statistical protocol (Agrawal et al., IST'18)
edges.ref: [2] A. Agrawal, W. Fu, and T. Menzies, "What is wrong with topic modeling? and how to fix it using search-based software engineering," IST, vol. 98, 2018.
edges.evidence: Here, we used those which have been past peer reviewed in the literature [2], [3]. Specifically, we use Efron's 95% confidence bootstrap procedure [18] and the A12 test [6].

edges.target: LDA-GA genetic-algorithm tuned LDA (Panichella et al., ICSE'13)
edges.ref: [48] A. Panichella, B. Dit, R. Oliveto, M. Di Penta, D. Poshyvanyk, and A. De Lucia, "How to effectively use topic models for software engineering tasks?" ICSE, 2013.
edges.evidence: LDAGA SVM used its own genetic algorithm ... DODGE(E) performs better than the ICSE'13 article that applied genetic algorithms to learn the settings for a text miner [48]

edges.target: Random search (Bergstra & Bengio)
edges.ref: [9] J. Bergstra and Y. Bengio, "Random search for hyper-parameter optimization," Journal of Machine Learning Research, 2012.
edges.evidence: a random search method that picks 30 random options (equivalent N as of DODGE(E)) from Table 1 ... random performs badly and never defeats DODGE(E).

edges.target: Differential evolution (Storn & Price)
edges.ref: [55] R. Storn and K. Price, "Differential evolution-a simple and efficient heuristic for global optimization over continuous spaces," J. Global Optimization, 1997.
edges.evidence: SMOTUNED uses differential evolutionary algorithm [55] ... LDADE FFT and LDADE SVM both used differential evolution [55].

edges.target: Scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al.)
edges.ref: [49] F. Pedregosa, G. Varoquaux, A. Gramfort, et al., "Scikit-learn: Machine learning in python," JMLR, vol. 12, 2011.
edges.evidence: consulting the documentation of a widely-used data mining library (Scikit-learn [49]) ... we use them with their defaults from Scikit-learn [49].

edges.target: NLTK toolkit (Bird)
edges.ref: [12] S. Bird, "Nltk: the natural language toolkit," in Proceedings of the COLING/ACL on Interactive presentation sessions, 2006, pp. 69-72.
edges.evidence: We implemented stop words removal using NLTK toolkit [12]
edges.section: 2.1.1 Data and Algorithms for Text Mining

edges.target: Porter stemmer
edges.ref: [52] M. Porter, "The Porter Stemming Algorithm," pp. 130-137, 1980. http://tartarus.org/martin/PorterStemmer/
edges.evidence: Next, Porter's stemming filter [52] was used to delete uninformative word endings
edges.section: 2.1.1 Data and Algorithms for Text Mining

edges.target: Standard text mining filters (Feldman, Text Mining Handbook)
edges.ref: [19] R.-S. Feldman, J, The Text Mining Handbook. New York: Cambridge University Press, 2006.
edges.evidence: For this study, all datasets were preprocessed using the usual text mining filters [19].

edges.target: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (Blei et al.)
edges.ref: [13] D. M. Blei, A. Y. Ng, and M. I. Jordan, "Latent dirichlet allocation," Journal of machine Learning research, vol. 3, 2003, pp. 993-1022.
edges.evidence: LatentDirichletAllocation(n components=a, ...) ... We studied LDA since it is a widely-used technique in prominent SE research articles [2].

edges.target: SMOTE (Chawla et al.)
edges.ref: [14] N. V. Chawla et al., "Smote: Synthetic minority over-sampling technique," J. Artif. Int. Res., 2002.
edges.evidence: A standard trick for class imbalance is SMOTE [14] that synthetically create members of the minority class. Table 1 show controlled parameters of SMOTE.

edges.target: NASA PITS issue-report text data (PitsA-F)
edges.ref: [34] T. Menzies, "Improving IV&V techniques through the analysis of project anomalies: Text mining pits issue reports-final report," 2008; [37] Menzies & Marcus, ICSM 2008.
edges.evidence: Table 2 describes our PITS data, which comes from six different NASA systems ... Data comes from the SEACRAFT repository: http://tiny.cc/seacraft

edges.target: SEACRAFT/PROMISE Java defect data (poi, lucene, camel, log4j, xerces, velocity, xalan, ivy, synapse, jedit)
edges.ref: http://tiny.cc/seacraft (no origin paper cited; metric definitions per table 1 of [3])
edges.evidence: Our defect predictors where applied to the data described in Table 6 ... this data is available for multiple software versions (from http://tiny.cc/seacraft).

edges.target: Popt at 20% of code (Ostrand et al.)
edges.ref: [46] T. J. Ostrand, E. J. Weyuker, and R. M. Bell, "Where the bugs are," in ACM SIGSOFT Software Engineering Notes. ACM, 2004.
edges.evidence: Following from the recommendations of Ostrand et al. [46], Popt is reported at the 20% point

edges.target: Normalized Popt (Kamei et al.; Yang et al.; Monden et al.)
edges.ref: [28] Y. Kamei et al., "A large-scale empirical study of just-in-time quality assurance," TSE 2013; [66] Y. Yang et al., FSE 2016; [40] Monden et al., TSE 2013.
edges.evidence: Kamei, Yang et al. [28], [40], [66] normalized Popt using: Popt(m) = 1 - (S(optimal) - S(m)) / (S(optimal) - S(worst))

edges.target: Cohen's d small-effect threshold
edges.ref: [16] J. Cohen, Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences. Routledge, 2013.
edges.evidence: To define "small effect", we use Cohen's delta [16]: d = small effect = 0.2 * sd ... i.e., 20% of the standard deviation.

edges.target: Efron 95% confidence bootstrap
edges.ref: [18] B. Efron and R. J. Tibshirani, An Introduction to the Bootstrap. New York: Chapman & Hall, 1993.
edges.evidence: Specifically, we use Efron's 95% confidence bootstrap procedure [18] and the A12 test [6].

edges.target: A12 effect size (Arcuri & Briand)
edges.ref: [6] A. Arcuri and L. Briand, "A practical guide for using statistical tests to assess randomized algorithms in software engineering," ICSE, 2011.
edges.evidence: then the A12 effect size test [6] (to demonstrate that the observed delta is bigger than a "small effect").

edges.target: Problems with precision (Menzies et al.)
edges.ref: [35] T. Menzies, A. Dekhtyar, J. Distefano, and J. Greenwald, "Problems with precision: A response to ...," IEEE TSE, 2007.
edges.evidence: We eschew precision and accuracy since these can be inaccurate for data sets where the target class is rare ... [35].

edges.target: epsilon-dominance / nature of SE data (Agrawal PhD dissertation)
edges.ref: [1] A. Agrawal, "On the nature of software engineering data (implications of ε-dominance in software engineering)," Ph.D. dissertation, NCSU, 2019.
edges.evidence: DODGE(E) is a method for learning what tunings are redundant; i.e., lead to results that are very similar to other tunings [1].

edges.target: Interactions with big data analytics (Fisher et al.)
edges.ref: [20] D. Fisher, R. DeLine, M. Czerwinski, and S. Drucker, "Interactions with big data analytics," ACM interactions, 2012.
edges.evidence: Fisher et al. [20] defines software analytics as a workflow ... Fisher et al warn that "the luxuries of interactivity, direct manipulation, and fast system response are gone".

edges.target: Grid-search tuning of defect predictors (Tantithamthavorn et al.)
edges.ref: [56] C. Tantithamthavorn, S. McIntosh, A. E. Hassan, K. Matsumoto, "The impact of automated parameter optimization on defect prediction models," TSE 45(7), 2019; [57] ICSE 2016.
edges.evidence: Despite this, some SE researchers persist in using grid search [56], [57]. ... DE's tandem search can outperform ... the grid search used by Tantithamthavorn et al.

edges.target: Parameter tuning or default values? (Arcuri & Fraser)
edges.ref: [7] A. Arcuri and G. Fraser, "Parameter tuning or default values? an empirical investigation in search-based software engineering," EMSE, 2013.
edges.evidence: We conjecture that if they used DODGE(E), then they could have explored more parameters and possibly reversed their conclusion that hyperparameter optimization adds little extra value.

edges.target: 12.7 CPU-weeks for 12,800 experiments (Panichella et al., ICST'15)
edges.ref: [47] A. Panichella, F. M. Kifetew, and P. Tonella, "Reformulating branch coverage as a many-objective optimization problem," ICST, 2015.
edges.evidence: their 12,800 experiments (each with a give-up time of 600 seconds), required 12.7 weeks of CPU to terminate.

edges.target: 1,000,000 test-suite evaluations for landscape analysis (Aleti et al.)
edges.ref: [5] A. Aleti, I. Moser, and L. Grunske, "Analysing the fitness landscape of search-based software testing problems," Automated Software Engineering, 2017.
edges.evidence: To learn the landscape associated with the test suites of 19 software programs, 30 times, Aleti et al. [5] evaluated 1,000,000 test suites.

edges.target: Practitioner survey: 90% willing to adopt defect prediction (Wan et al.)
edges.ref: [61] Z. Wan, X. Xia, A. E. Hassan, D. Lo, J. Yin, and X. Yang, "Perceptions, expectations, and challenges in defect prediction," IEEE TSE, 2018.
edges.evidence: In a survey of 395 practitioners from 33 countries and five continents, Wan et al. [61] found that over 90% of the respondents were willing to adopt defect prediction

edges.target: Industrial defect predictor: 87% predicted, 72% less inspection (Misirli et al.)
edges.ref: [39] A. T. Misirli, A. Bener, and R. Kale, "Ai-based software defect predictors: Applications and benefits in a case study," IAAI, 2010.
edges.evidence: those models could predict 87% of files with defects. Those models also decreased inspection efforts by 72%, and hence reduced post-release defects by 44%.

edges.target: Static bug finders vs statistical prediction (Rahman et al., ICSE'14)
edges.ref: [53] F. Rahman, S. Khatri, E. T. Barr, and P. Devanbu, "Comparing static bug finders and statistical prediction," ICSE, 2014.
edges.evidence: They found no significant differences in the cost-effectiveness of these approaches.

edges.target: 80% of business on unstructured data (White)
edges.ref: [63] C. White, "Consolidating, accessing and analyzing unstructured data," 2005, http://www.b-eye-network.com/view/2098.
edges.evidence: According to White [63], 80% of business is conducted on unstructured data, 85% of all data stored is held in an unstructured format

not_reuse_examples: [4] Agrawal et al. DUO literature review — pointed to as 'elsewhere we offer an extensive literature review'; not used in the experiments.
[17] NSGA-II, [70] IBEA, [68] MOEA/D, [43] FLASH — listed as examples of 21st-century optimizers; none is run or compared against.

[11] Binkley et al. SE-specific NLP — cited only as a 'similar conclusion' in the discussion; [60] Vesterstrom & Thomsen and [25]/[29] GA/SA textbooks are background on why DE was chosen inside the baselines.
notes: Empirical SE tools paper (TSE/arXiv 2019) introducing the DODGE(E) hyperparameter optimizer; heavily self-reusing (FFtrees, SMOTUNED, DE+RF, LDADE, PITS data all from Menzies-group); Fig. 3 is reprinted from Chen et al. [15]; defect data origin paper (Jureczko) not cited, only the SEACRAFT repo URL.
